item.title: Code Lies, Facts Don't, Part 2: The Method
item.description: Sridharan's method for debugging code you can't read: facts as fixed constraints and hypotheses that must satisfy every one, controls and 'sad paths', a hypotheses-by-fact table that ranks clues, five tactics for repairing broken theories, and descending layers for new signals. Why AI-made repros and same-model reviews are weaker safeguards than they look, why demanding citations works, and her 'agent-native software factory' that counts every human intervention as a gap.

item.title: Code Lies, Facts Don't, Part 1: Three Bugs
item.description: Cindy Sridharan argues code is an unreliable narrator: it tells you what can happen, not what did. Three real bugs she debugged with an AI agent: a latency spike where a plausible certificate theory passed review but was wrong, and the real clue was 5 versus 400 DNS addresses; a memory leak that took three wrong answers and turned out to have two causes; and a hang found four layers down, in one line of a 30 MB kernel dump. Source: her Medium essay 'How to effectively debug when you no longer understand the code,' via an IntuiBloom knowledge graph.

item.title: Models as Insiders, Part 2: Who Watches the Watcher
item.description: What if the thing checking an AI model is another black box? Nadella's nested-black-box warning, his call for chain-of-thought transparency, and his model-diversity rule, set against the map's counterweights: research showing explanations aren't always faithful, the 1986 Knight and Leveson experiment where independent software versions failed together, AI control research, interpretability, the ironies of automation, and the standards and liability layers where containment gets enforced.

item.title: Models as Insiders, Part 1: The Insider Frame
item.description: Satya Nadella argues frontier AI models should be governed as privileged insiders: not because they are malicious, but because anything that capable with that much access can err or be compromised. We cover his split between the supply of intelligence and authority over it, containment-first engineering, and his seven observability principles. Then we flag the map's own background additions: insider threat programs, Saltzer and Schroeder, Ken Thompson's Trusting Trust, and the principal-agent problem. Source: Nadella's X article 'Models as Insider Risks in the Super Intelligence Era,' via an IntuiBloom knowledge graph.

item.title: Mining the Sky, Part 1: The Jar and the Asteroid
item.description: Devon Eriksen's viral post, replying to Elon Musk, argues Earth's valuable metals sank to the core and the ones we mine came from asteroids. We unpack his jar thought experiment and the real science under it (planetary differentiation, Goldschmidt's element classes, the late veneer), then the knowledge map's main pushback: 'every mine is an asteroid strike' is right about where the atoms came from but mostly wrong about how ore deposits form. Plus why the post's combative tone matters.

item.title: Hiring in the Age of AI, Part 1: What Survived the Interview Lab
item.description: JD Pruett's 20/10 philosophy: when coding agents eat the middle 70% of a project, hire for the first 20% (framing, architecture, taste) and the last 10% (shipping). We walk through the interview formats he tried and dropped — the agent-assisted long onsite, the AI systems design round, rule-of-thumb trivia — and the two that survived: unassisted code review with 'what if' changes, and an onsite that opens with a market presentation and then three shrinking timed problems, all judged by whether interviewers can give a confident thumbs up or down.

item.title: Prediction Markets, Part 2: When the Price Lies
item.description: Part 2 opens with a quick recap, then a March 2025 Polymarket market on a Ukraine minerals deal that, per news reports, resolved 'yes' with no deal signed after a token-holder vote. We cover the favorite-longshot bias (prices act like betting odds in the tails), wash trading and why volume isn't proof (estimates vary widely), oracles as the real point of centralization, and the parallel with catastrophe-bond triggers. Then the rivals: the Good Judgment Project's superforecasters and no-money platforms like Metaculus and Manifold, where the comparisons are messy. We close with futarchy, Hanson's untested idea to 'vote on values, bet on beliefs.' Not betting or investment advice.

item.title: Prediction Markets, Part 1: How a Price Becomes a Forecast
item.description: Part 1 of a two-parter built from a knowledge graph on prediction markets. A contract pays one dollar if an event happens, so its price reads as a probability. We cover why economists think that should work (Hayek's idea that prices pool scattered knowledge, plus Arrow-Debreu and efficient markets), the automated market maker that keeps thin markets trading, corporate markets at firms like Google, and how the law shaped the field: Iowa Electronic Markets, Intrade's shutdown, Polymarket's exit and 2025 return, and Kalshi's court win. We end with catastrophe bonds as an older, professional version of the same idea. Dated events were checked against news coverage. Not betting or investment advice.

item.title: Cancer's Second Verb: Converting Tumors Instead of Killing Them
item.description: A walk through a knowledge graph built from Brian Roemmele's X post on a KAIST study (Advanced Science, 2024). As the post tells it, researchers built a 'digital twin' of an intestinal cell's gene network, used an algorithm called BENEIN to pick three genes (MYB, HDAC2, FOXA2), and turned colon cancer cells into normal-like cells in cell lines and mice by maturing them rather than killing them. This is early preclinical work with no human data, described secondhand, and nothing here is medical advice. The graph adds context: differentiation therapy has treated the leukemia APL for decades, the idea builds on Waddington, Kauffman and Yamanaka, and hard-to-drug targets, durability (speculative) and the tumor's surroundings could keep it from becoming a therapy.

item.title: How to Research Anything, Part 2: Why It Works
item.description: Part 2 opens with a quick recap of the method, then looks at why it might work and where it falls short. The knowledge graph adds outside theories, all flagged as interpretation: the guide's 'plateau of diminishing returns' mirrors ecology's rule for when a forager should leave a patch, 'useful a year from now?' estimates how fast a field's facts go stale, and a pre-set 'done' is Herbert Simon's satisficing. Then two tensions the guide leaves unaddressed: AI summaries may erode the outsider's fresh eyes, and expert calls aren't independent witnesses. We close with cross-domain synthesis and the author's compounding research playbook.

item.title: The Slop Superhighway
item.description: Rhys Sullivan argues that agents flooding human channels like GitHub issues isn't the real failure. The failure is that there's no agent-to-agent channel to carry that traffic, so humans end up as 'meat proxies' copy-pasting between AIs. We walk through his first-person Cloudflare bug story (single-sourced), the 2025 issueslop backlash, what exists today (author-side issue triage, MCP, A2A), and what's still missing: identity, payments, and defenses against prompt injection. We close with economics and liability lenses, which the knowledge graph adds as its own speculative extensions rather than claims from the post.

The failure is that there's no agent-to-agent channel to carry that traffic, so humans end up as 'meat proxies' copy-pasting between AIs. We walk through his first-person Cloudflare bug story (single-sourced), the 2025 issueslop backlash, what exists today (author-side issue triage, MCP, A2A), and what's still missing: identity, payments, and defenses against prompt injection. We close with economics and liability lenses, which the knowledge graph adds as its own speculative extensions rather than claims from the post.

item.title: Super Is Not Superior
item.description: A deep dive into Tejas Kumar's essay "AI Is Now SI: Super Intelligence Isn't Superior," via a knowledge graph of its argument. The essay says "super" describes task performance while "superior" claims worth, and that renaming AI "Super Intelligence" blurs the two. Covers Bostrom's definition of superintelligence, real machine milestones, the BCG "jagged frontier" study, the golden calf, Calvin's "forge of idols," the sun renamed "the greater light" in Genesis, and the essay's case for loyalty as a willingness to overpay. 2026 events are as reported in the essay.

item.title: Fine-Tuning at Home: Beat Frontier Models With 8 Steps
item.description: A two-host walkthrough of a knowledge graph built from Maxime Rivest's article "Even you can now fine-tune an LLM, and maybe you finally should." The claim: with a coding agent, a frontier "teacher" model and LoRA adapters on consumer hardware, fine-tuning a task-specific model is now something one person can do. Covers the eight-step workflow, synthetic distillation, why training loss kept improving while rubric scores plateaued, the roughly 1,000-example saturation point, the break-even math (about 170 papers per hour), licensing limits on training with model outputs, and the last-mile accuracy problem. Benchmark figures are the author's own reported results.
